claim: Single-particle tracking (SPT) directly measures the dynamics of proteins in living cells.
source: Single-particle tracking (SPT) directly measures the dynamics of proteins in living cells and is a powerful tool to dissect molecular mechanisms of cellular regulation.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract describing the purpose and capability of SPT.

claim: Interpretation of SPT with fast-diffusing proteins in mammalian cells is complicated by short trajectory length due to photobleaching and shallow depth of field.
source: Interpretation of SPT with fast-diffusing proteins in mammalian cells, however, is complicated by technical limitations imposed by fast image acquisition. These limitations include short trajectory length due to photobleaching and shallow depth of field, high localization error due to the low photon budget imposed by short integration times, and cell-to-cell variability.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states these technical limitations in the abstract.

claim: High localization error in SPT is due to the low photon budget imposed by short integration times.
source: These limitations include short trajectory length due to photobleaching and shallow depth of field, high localization error due to the low photon budget imposed by short integration times, and cell-to-cell variability.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly identifies the cause of high localization error.

claim: Some interactions such as complex formation cause changes in a molecule's mobility.
source: Some interactions – such as complex formation – cause changes in a molecule's mobility.
evidence: This is stated as a known relationship between molecular interactions and mobility.

claim: Live-cell single-particle tracking is a promising tool to measure subpopulations of molecules engaged in distinct interactions without perturbing the living system.
source: As a result, live-cell single-particle tracking (SPT), by separately observing the motion of individual molecules, is a promising tool to meet this challenge (Shen et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites Shen et al., 2017 to support this claim about SPT's utility.

claim: SPT originally targeted proteins on cellular membranes.
source: While SPT originally targeted proteins on cellular membranes, advances in the past two decades led to intracellular applications (Barak and Webb, 1982, Ghosh and Webb, 1994, Kubitscheck et al., 2000, Goulian and Simon, 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple historical references to support the original application of SPT.

claim: Advances in the past two decades led to intracellular applications of SPT.
source: While SPT originally targeted proteins on cellular membranes, advances in the past two decades led to intracellular applications (Barak and Webb, 1982, Ghosh and Webb, 1994, Kubitscheck et al., 2000, Goulian and Simon, 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references documenting the evolution to intracellular applications.

claim: Stochastic labeling can be used to isolate a single emitter's path.
source: These include the use of stochastic labeling to isolate a single emitter's path (Manley et al., 2008), a principle that can be extended into intracellular settings with genetically encoded photoconvertible proteins (Ando et al., 2002, Wiedenmann et al., 2004) or cell-permeable dyes (Grimm et al., 2015, Grimm et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites Manley et al., 2008 as the source for this technique.

claim: Pulsed or 'stroboscopic' excitation reduces blur associated with fast-diffusing emitters.
source: Another advance is pulsed or 'stroboscopic' excitation, which reduces blur associated with fast-diffusing emitters (Elf et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites Elf et al., 2007 to support this claim about stroboscopic excitation.

claim: Apparent motion in sptPALM reflects both the true motion of the emitter and localization error.
source: First, apparent motion in sptPALM reflects both the true motion of the emitter and error associated with the estimate for its position ('localization error') (Martin et al., 2002, Matsuoka et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites Martin et al., 2002 and Matsuoka et al., 2009 to support this claim.

claim: The magnitude of localization error in sptPALM depends on the number of photons collected from each emitter.
source: Like fixed cell PALM and STORM microscopies (Betzig et al., 2006, Rust et al., 2006), the magnitude of localization error in sptPALM depends on the number of photons collected from each emitter (Thompson et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript cites Thompson et al., 2002 to support this relationship.

claim: sptPALM has a component of error due to motion blur, which is the convolution of the microscope's point spread function with the path of the emitter.
source: But unlike fixed cell microscopies, sptPALM has another component of error due to motion blur, the convolution of the microscope's point spread function with the path of the emitter.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines motion blur as a source of error in sptPALM.

claim: The mean 2D displacement of a Brownian particle with diffusion coefficient 10 μm2 s-1 during a 1 ms integration is ~180 nm.
source: This component of error is not trivial: the mean 2D displacement of a Brownian particle with diffusion coefficient 10 μm2 s-1 during a 1 ms integration is ~180 nm, substantially larger than typical localization error in fixed cell PALM/STORM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript provides a calculated value and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1B for visual support.

claim: Localization error in sptPALM depends on both the emitter's mobility and its distance from the focus.
source: Consequently, localization error in sptPALM depends on both the emitter's mobility and its distance from the focus and is not simple to measure (Kubitscheck et al., 2000, Berglund, 2010, Michalet and Berglund, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references to support this claim about the complexity of localization error.

claim: High numerical aperture objectives required to resolve single emitters induce short depths of field, typically less than a micron.
source: Second, the high numerical aperture (NA) objectives required to resolve single emitters induce short depths of field, typically less than a micron.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a known property of high NA objectives.

claim: Bacteria such as Escherichia coli are often small enough to fit into the focal volume.
source: Whereas bacteria such as Escherichia coli are often small enough to fit into the resulting focal volume, mammalian cells – with depths ≥5–10 μm – cannot.
evidence: The manuscript contrasts bacterial and mammalian cell sizes relative to focal volume.

claim: Mammalian cells have depths ≥5–10 μm.
source: Whereas bacteria such as Escherichia coli are often small enough to fit into the resulting focal volume, mammalian cells – with depths ≥5–10 μm – cannot.
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific size range for mammalian cells.

claim: Intracellular SPT experiments only capture short transits of emitters through the focal volume, a behavior termed defocalization.
source: As a result, intracellular SPT experiments only capture short transits of emitters through the focal volume, a behavior termed defocalization (Figure 1C, Video 2, Video 3; Kues and Kubitscheck, 2002, Mazza et al., 2012, Hansen et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript defines defocalization and cites supporting references and figures.

claim: The duration of each transit through the focal volume depends on the emitter's mobility.
source: The duration of each transit depends on the emitter's mobility.
evidence: The manuscript states this relationship between mobility and transit duration.

claim: Mean trajectory length in sptPALM is often as little as 3–4 frames.
source: Mean trajectory length is often as little as 3–4 frames, severely limiting the ability to infer dynamic parameters (such as diffusion coefficient) from any single trajectory.
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific range for typical trajectory lengths.

claim: A common approach to recover subpopulations from sptPALM is to construct histograms of the mean squared displacement (MSD).
source: A common approach to recover subpopulations from sptPALM is to construct histograms of the mean squared displacement (MSD), the maximum likelihood estimator for the diffusion coefficient in the absence of localization error.
evidence: The manuscript describes a commonly used method in the field.

claim: The MSD is the maximum likelihood estimator for the diffusion coefficient in the absence of localization error.
source: A common approach to recover subpopulations from sptPALM is to construct histograms of the mean squared displacement (MSD), the maximum likelihood estimator for the diffusion coefficient in the absence of localization error.
evidence: The manuscript states this statistical property of the MSD.

claim: The MSD is highly variable for short trajectories.
source: The MSD is highly variable for short trajectories and, when used to estimate diffusion coefficient, becomes especially error-prone when the variance of localization error is unknown (Michalet and Berglund, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites Michalet and Berglund, 2012 to support this limitation of MSD.

claim: MSD histograms assume that sampling from slow and fast states with equal occupation produces the same number of trajectories.
source: More problematically, MSD histograms assume that sampling from slow and fast states with equal occupation produces the same number of trajectories, which leads to severe state biases in the presence of defocalization (Mazza et al., 2012, Hansen et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites Mazza et al., 2012 and Hansen et al., 2018 to support this problematic assumption.

claim: Methods based on least-squares fitting of the jump length cumulative distribution function have interpreted sptPALM data with two- and three-state models while accounting for defocalization.
source: Methods based on least-squares fitting of the jump length cumulative distribution function (CDF) have interpreted sptPALM data with two- and three-state models while accounting for defocalization (Mazza et al., 2012, Hansen et al., 2018), but extend poorly to more complex models due to overfitting and do not provide a way to select between competing models.
evidence: The manuscript cites Mazza et al., 2012 and Hansen et al., 2018 to describe these methods.

claim: vbSPT is a variational Bayesian framework for reaction-diffusion models.
source: A different approach to model selection is represented by vbSPT, a variational Bayesian framework for reaction-diffusion models (Persson et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites Persson et al., 2013 to describe vbSPT.

claim: vbSPT relies on the evidence lower bound to identify the number of states.
source: vbSPT relies on the evidence lower bound to identify the number of states, and it excels at recovering occupations and transition rates for a small number of diffusing states from short trajectories.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodology of vbSPT.

claim: vbSPT does not consider defocalization or localization error.
source: However, it is not appropriate to apply in situations where the target's dynamic profile is not discrete and does not consider defocalization or localization error, although it can be complemented with a separate estimate of localization error (Lindén et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites Lindén et al., 2017 to describe limitations of vbSPT.

claim: State arrays (SAs) far outperformed DPMMs when evaluated on real sptPALM data.
source: Between the two methods, SAs far outperformed DPMMs.
evidence: The manuscript states this comparative result from their analysis.

claim: SAs revealed previously unappreciated features of the dynamic profile for RARA-HaloTag and H2B-HaloTag.
source: When evaluated on real sptPALM data, SAs revealed previously unappreciated features of the dynamic profile for RARA-HaloTag and H2B-HaloTag.
evidence: The manuscript describes novel findings from applying SAs to experimental data.

claim: RARA-HaloTag exhibited a broad spectrum of diffusive states.
source: In particular, RARA-HaloTag exhibited a broad spectrum of diffusive states that stands in contrast to the more discretized profile of H2B-HaloTag or HaloTag-NLS.
evidence: The manuscript describes the observed dynamic profile of RARA-HaloTag.

claim: H2B-HaloTag has a more discretized profile compared to RARA-HaloTag.
source: In particular, RARA-HaloTag exhibited a broad spectrum of diffusive states that stands in contrast to the more discretized profile of H2B-HaloTag or HaloTag-NLS.
evidence: The manuscript contrasts the dynamic profiles of different proteins.

claim: The SA method is publicly available as the pip-installable Python package saspt.
source: The SA method is publicly available as the pip-installable Python package saspt (source: https://github.com/alecheckert/saspt; Heckert, 2022c documentation: https://saspt.readthedocs.io/en/latest/).
evidence: The manuscript provides information about software availability.

claim: Addition of the NLS reduces HaloTag's diffusion coefficient by two- to threefold.
source: In agreement with previous reports (Xiang et al., 2020), we observed that addition of the NLS reduces HaloTag's diffusion coefficient by two- to threefold.
evidence: The manuscript cites Xiang et al., 2020 and reports their own observation.

claim: RARA-HT has an immobile fraction accounting for roughly 40% of its total population.
source: In contrast, both RARA-HT and H2B-HT had substantial immobile fractions, accounting for roughly 40 and 70% of their total populations, respectively (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data and references Figure 5C.

claim: H2B-HT has an immobile fraction accounting for roughly 70% of its total population.
source: In contrast, both RARA-HT and H2B-HT had substantial immobile fractions, accounting for roughly 40 and 70% of their total populations, respectively (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data and references Figure 5C.

claim: H2B-HT presented a fast population at 8–10 μm2 s-1.
source: Whereas H2B-HT presented a fast population at 8–10 μm2 s-1, RARA-HT inhabited a broad spectrum of diffusing states ranging from 0.3 to 10.0 μm2 s-1.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific diffusion coefficient values for H2B-HT.

claim: RARA-HT inhabited a broad spectrum of diffusing states ranging from 0.3 to 10.0 μm2 s-1.
source: Whereas H2B-HT presented a fast population at 8–10 μm2 s-1, RARA-HT inhabited a broad spectrum of diffusing states ranging from 0.3 to 10.0 μm2 s-1.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific diffusion coefficient ranges for RARA-HT.

claim: Removal of either the DNA-binding domain (DBD) or LBD of RARA-HT resulted in loss of the immobile population.
source: Removal of either the DNA-binding domain (DBD) or LBD resulted in loss of the immobile population.
evidence: The manuscript describes the results of domain deletion experiments.

claim: Both the DBD and LBD are required for chromatin binding by the RAR/RXR heterodimer.
source: Because both the DBD and LBD are required for chromatin binding by the RAR/RXR heterodimer, this suggests that the immobile fraction represents chromatin-bound molecules.
evidence: The manuscript uses known requirements for chromatin binding to interpret their results.

claim: The immobile fraction of RARA-HT represents chromatin-bound molecules.
source: Because both the DBD and LBD are required for chromatin binding by the RAR/RXR heterodimer, this suggests that the immobile fraction represents chromatin-bound molecules.
evidence: The manuscript infers this interpretation from domain deletion results.

claim: A point mutation (C88G) in the zinc fingers for the RARA-HT DBD abolishes DNA-binding in vitro.
source: To confirm this, we introduced a point mutation (C88G) in the zinc fingers for the RARA-HT DBD that abolishes DNA-binding in vitro (Zhu et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites Zhu et al., 1999 to support the effect of this mutation.

claim: The C88G mutation in RARA-HT led to loss of the immobile fraction.
source: This led to loss of the immobile fraction (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of the C88G mutation experiment and references Figure 5B.

claim: Deletion of the unstructured N-terminal domain (NTD) or C-terminal domain (CTD) of RARA-HT had a milder effect.
source: Deletion of the unstructured N-terminal domain (NTD) or C-terminal domain (CTD) had a milder effect, suggesting that these domains are not the primary determinants of the dynamic behavior of RARA-HT.
evidence: The manuscript describes the results of NTD and CTD deletion experiments.

claim: The primary origins of variability for both DPMMs and SAs were cell-to-cell rather than clone-to-clone variability or intrinsic variability due to finite sample sizes.
source: The primary origins of variability for both DPMMs and SAs were cell-to-cell rather than clone-to-clone variability or intrinsic variability due to finite sample sizes.
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of bootstrap aggregation experiments.

claim: NPM1-HT exhibits partial nucleolar localization.
source: We explored this aspect of SAs with a U2OS nucleophosmin-HaloTag (NPM1-HT) sptPALM dataset. NPM1-HT exhibits partial nucleolar localization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) and distinct dynamic behavior inside and outside nucleoli (Mitrea et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites Mitrea et al., 2018 and references Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NPM1-HT has distinct dynamic behavior inside and outside nucleoli.
source: NPM1-HT exhibits partial nucleolar localization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) and distinct dynamic behavior inside and outside nucleoli (Mitrea et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites Mitrea et al., 2018 to support this claim.

claim: The SA identified a broad range of diffusion coefficients for NPM1-HT, with three modes including an effectively immobile population.
source: The SA identified a broad range of diffusion coefficients for NPM1-HT, with three modes including an effectively immobile population (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of SA analysis and references Figure 6A.

claim: A slow-moving mobile population at 0.23 μm2 s-1 is enriched in nucleoli.
source: This analysis revealed that some populations (including a slow-moving mobile population at 0.23 μm2 s-1) are enriched in nucleoli, while others (for instance, a fast-moving population at 4 μm2 s-1) are depleted and still others show no preference (Figure 6C).
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial analysis results and references Figure 6C.

claim: A fast-moving population at 4 μm2 s-1 is depleted in nucleoli.
source: This analysis revealed that some populations (including a slow-moving mobile population at 0.23 μm2 s-1) are enriched in nucleoli, while others (for instance, a fast-moving population at 4 μm2 s-1) are depleted and still others show no preference (Figure 6C).
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial analysis results and references Figure 6C.

claim: High localization densities led to a deflation in the occupation of slower-moving states, probably due to tracking errors.
source: These experiments demonstrated that high localization densities led to a deflation in the occupation of slower-moving states, probably due to tracking errors.
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation and provides a probable explanation.

claim: DPMMs and SAs do not deal with transitions between states.
source: Both methods share the limitation that they do not deal with transitions between states.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this limitation of both methods.

claim: SAs can be applied to any motion model parameterized by a likelihood function.
source: While our investigation focused primarily on Brownian motion, SAs can be applied to any motion model parameterized by a likelihood function.
evidence: The manuscript states the general applicability of SAs.

claim: Fractional Brownian motion (FBM) is a generalization of Brownian motion capable of producing anomalous diffusion.
source: To explore applications of SAs outside of Brownian motion, we applied it to fractional Brownian motion (FBM), a generalization of Brownian motion capable of producing anomalous diffusion (Mandelbrot and Van Ness, 1968).
evidence: The manuscript cites Mandelbrot and Van Ness, 1968 to describe FBM.

claim: Brownian motion's sole parameter is the diffusion coefficient.
source: Whereas Brownian motion's sole parameter is the diffusion coefficient, FBM parameterizes both the magnitude (via a scaling coefficient) and the temporal correlations (via the Hurst parameter) of a particle's increments.
evidence: The manuscript contrasts Brownian motion with FBM.

claim: FBM parameterizes both the magnitude (via a scaling coefficient) and the temporal correlations (via the Hurst parameter) of a particle's increments.
source: Whereas Brownian motion's sole parameter is the diffusion coefficient, FBM parameterizes both the magnitude (via a scaling coefficient) and the temporal correlations (via the Hurst parameter) of a particle's increments.
evidence: The manuscript describes the parameters of FBM.

claim: The SA accurately recovered the diffusion coefficient and Hurst parameter for multistate FBM models.
source: While the SA accurately recovered the diffusion coefficient and Hurst parameter for multistate FBM models (Figure 4—figure supplement 11D), we noted a systematic error in the estimation of low (subdiffusive) Hurst parameters due to motion blur (Figure 4—figure supplement 12).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of SA analysis on FBM and references figures.

claim: There is a systematic error in the estimation of low (subdiffusive) Hurst parameters due to motion blur.
source: While the SA accurately recovered the diffusion coefficient and Hurst parameter for multistate FBM models (Figure 4—figure supplement 11D), we noted a systematic error in the estimation of low (subdiffusive) Hurst parameters due to motion blur (Figure 4—figure supplement 12).
evidence: The manuscript reports this systematic error and references Figure 4—figure supplement 12.

claim: RARA-HT is a type II nuclear receptor that heterodimerizes via its ligand-binding domain (LBD) with the retinoid X receptor (RXR) to form a complex competent to bind chromatin and regulate target genes.
source: RARA-HT is a type II nuclear receptor that heterodimerizes via its ligand-binding domain (LBD) with the retinoid X receptor (RXR) to form a complex competent to bind chromatin and regulate target genes Giguere et al., 1987, Petkovich et al., 1987, Brand et al., 1988, Yu et al., 1991, Bugge et al., 1992, Marks et al., 1992, Leid et al., 1992; reviewed in Evans and Mangelsdorf, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references to describe RARA-HT function.

claim: Association of coregulator complexes with the RAR/RXR heterodimer has been shown to influence the dimer's dynamics in FCS studies.
source: In addition, association of coregulator complexes with the RAR/RXR heterodimer has been shown to influence the dimer's dynamics in FCS studies (Brazda et al., 2011, Brazda et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Brazda et al., 2011 and Brazda et al., 2014 to support this claim.

claim: H2B-HT is a protein with a high-occupation immobile state.
source: For comparison, we also performed identical sptPALM experiments with histone H2B-HaloTag (H2B-HT), a protein with a high-occupation immobile state (Hansen et al., 2017, McSwiggen et al., 2019), as well as HaloTag and HaloTag-NLS (HT and HT-NLS), which are fast-diffusing proteins with low immobile fractions.
evidence: The manuscript cites Hansen et al., 2017 and McSwiggen et al., 2019 to describe H2B-HT.

claim: HaloTag and HaloTag-NLS are fast-diffusing proteins with low immobile fractions.
source: For comparison, we also performed identical sptPALM experiments with histone H2B-HaloTag (H2B-HT), a protein with a high-occupation immobile state (Hansen et al., 2017, McSwiggen et al., 2019), as well as HaloTag and HaloTag-NLS (HT and HT-NLS), which are fast-diffusing proteins with low immobile fractions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the properties of HT and HT-NLS.

claim: For both HT and HT-NLS, the SA identified a single highly mobile state.
source: For both HT and HT-NLS, the SA identified a single highly mobile state.
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of SA analysis on HT and HT-NLS.

claim: SAs require selection of a parameter grid with spacing fine enough to avoid discretization artifacts.
source: DPMMs require prior measurement of the localization error, while SAs require selection of a parameter grid with spacing fine enough to avoid discretization artifacts.
evidence: The manuscript states this requirement for SAs.

claim: DPMMs require prior measurement of the localization error.
source: DPMMs require prior measurement of the localization error, while SAs require selection of a parameter grid with spacing fine enough to avoid discretization artifacts.
evidence: The manuscript states this requirement for DPMMs.

claim: Neither DPMMs nor SAs consider transitions between states.
source: Additionally, neither DPMMs nor SAs consider transitions between states, a major shortcoming of these methods.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this limitation.

claim: The experiments used a fixed range of diffusion coefficients from 10-2 to 102 μm2 s-1.
source: Our experiments used a fixed range of diffusion coefficients from 10-2 to 102 μm2 s-1.
evidence: The manuscript states the range used in their experiments.

claim: When the true diffusion coefficient was outside the range 10-2 to 102 μm2 s-1, SAs accurately estimated state occupations by using the nearest available diffusion coefficient.
source: Even when the true diffusion coefficient was outside this range, SAs accurately estimated state occupations by using the nearest available diffusion coefficient (Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
evidence: The manuscript reports this result and references Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claim: Experimental SPT results with large spikes at the lowest diffusion coefficient suggest that true diffusion coefficients outside the support range are common in real data for SPT targets with very slow or immobile populations.
source: Our experimental SPT results, with large spikes at the lowest diffusion coefficient, suggest this is common in real data for SPT targets with very slow or immobile populations.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from their experimental observations.

claim: The SA's size scales with the number of parameters of the motion.
source: First, the SA's size scales with the number of parameters of the motion, meaning that more complex models are more computationally expensive.
evidence: The manuscript states this computational property of SAs.

claim: Both the Hurst parameter in FBM and the localization error primarily manifest as negative off-diagonal components of the trajectory increment covariance matrix.
source: For instance, both the Hurst parameter in FBM and the localization error primarily manifest as negative off-diagonal components of the trajectory increment covariance matrix (Figure 4—figure supplement 11B).
evidence: The manuscript describes this similarity and references Figure 4—figure supplement 11B.

claim: In a recent objective evaluation of methods to measure anomalous diffusion, even top-performing methods were associated with mean absolute error >0.3 when estimating anomaly parameters for short trajectories (<10 frames).
source: In a recent objective evaluation of methods to measure anomalous diffusion (Muñoz-Gil et al., 2021), even top-performing methods (including recent machine learning approaches) were associated with mean absolute error gt0.3 when estimating anomaly parameters for short trajectories (<10 frames).
evidence: The manuscript cites Muñoz-Gil et al., 2021 to support this claim about method performance.

claim: Neither DPMMs nor SAs have any built-in mechanism to distinguish true jumps from tracking errors.
source: Neither DPMMs nor SAs have any built-in mechanism to distinguish true jumps from tracking errors.
evidence: The manuscript states this limitation of both methods.

claim: Both DPMMs and SAs rely on trajectories produced by another algorithm.
source: Both rely on trajectories produced by another algorithm.
evidence: The manuscript states this dependency of both methods.
